subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

periods.activity_title: A Walk Through Plants: Noticing Trees Around Us
periods.textbook_anchor: So Many Kinds of Plants — Students write names of trees they recognise and recall where they have seen them (p. 49)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations of mango, coconut, banyan, peepal, and chinar trees (p. 49)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud the opening story of three children walking to school, pausing to invite students to name any plant, tree or leaf they notice on their own walk to school. The class shares sensory details — shade, smell, colour — they have experienced.

Students open Textbook p. 49 and look at the illustrations of trees. The teacher introduces the defining features of trees: one big woody trunk, deep roots, and many branches. Students discuss which trees from the page they have seen and where — near home, on a road, in a park.

Students write in their notebooks the names of trees they can recognise, noting where each was seen, as invited on Textbook p. 49. The teacher circulates, prompting students to include details about the tree's size, bark texture, or smell if they remember.

Pairs share their lists with each other and the class compiles a short collective list on the board — trees seen near school versus near home. The teacher closes by asking students what makes a tree different from other plants, drawing out the idea of one big woody trunk.

periods.implied_lo: Students can recall and describe familiar plants in their surroundings using sensory details and location.
periods.section_context: Mango, coconut, khejri, jackfruit, banyan, amaltas, peepal, chinar trees; sensory features — texture, smell, shade, colour of leaves and fruits.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone ever touched the bark of a tree or smelled its fruit while walking somewhere — what did it feel like or smell like?' This invites rich sensory language and naturally surfaces local tree names children know from home.

periods.activity_title: Shrubs in Our World: Names, Features, and Food Connections
periods.textbook_anchor: Shrubs — Students write names of shrubs and identify them in the pictures (p. 50)
materials: Sample sprigs or leaves of tulsi or curry leaf if available in the school garden
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations of hibiscus, rose, tulsi, and curry leaf shrubs (p. 50)

time_bands.activity: The teacher holds up (or points to a picture of) a tulsi or hibiscus plant and asks students to describe what they notice — how many stems, how tall, whether the stems feel hard or soft. Students share what they already know about these plants and where they grow.

Students open Textbook p. 50 and examine the illustrations. The teacher explains what makes a shrub: several woody stems growing close to the ground, medium height, distinct from the single big trunk of a tree. Students compare a shrub and a tree aloud — what is the same, what is different.

Students write the names of shrubs they have seen in their notebooks, as invited on Textbook p. 50, including what the plant is called in their mother tongue. The teacher prompts: 'Have you seen any of these plants at home, in a garden, or near a temple or kitchen?' This draws out the everyday cultural presence of tulsi and curry leaf.

The teacher introduces the food connection: toor, masoor, moong, and urad dal — familiar in everyday Indian meals — come from shrubs. The class discusses which of these they eat at home and what the cooked dish looks like, connecting a plant type to a daily food tradition. The unit closes with students naming one shrub and one food that comes from it.

periods.implied_lo: Students can distinguish shrubs from trees using observable physical features and connect plant types to everyday uses.
periods.section_context: Hibiscus, rose, tulsi (holy basil), curry leaf; toor, masoor, moong, urad dal as seeds of shrubs; mother-tongue names.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'What do we call tulsi or curry leaf at home — do different families have different names for them?' This opens space for mother-tongue vocabulary and the cultural role of these plants in Indian households.

periods.activity_title: Herbs and Grasses: Soft Stems and Surprising Food Grains
periods.textbook_anchor: Herbs and Grasses — Students write names of herbs they have seen and where (p. 52)
materials: A sprig of mint or coriander if available
A small sample of wheat grain or a drawing of paddy if available
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations of mint, tomato, coriander, mustard, paddy, wheat, bajra, jowar, ragi, sugarcane, and bamboo (p. 52)

time_bands.activity: The teacher passes around a sprig of mint or coriander (or shows a close-up picture) and asks students to describe the stem — is it hard or soft, thick or thin? Students predict: could this plant stand tall without support? This builds the concept of a soft stem before naming it.

Students open Textbook p. 52. The teacher explains herbs (smaller plants, soft stems that do not become woody) and grasses (a type of herb with thin, flat, hollow-stemmed leaves). Students observe the illustrations and note which plants they recognise — mint, tomato, coriander, mustard — and where they have seen them.

Students write in their notebooks the names of herbs they have seen and where, as invited on Textbook p. 52. The teacher then draws attention to the food grain connection: paddy, wheat, bajra, jowar, and ragi — staple foods — are seeds of large grasses; sugarcane and bamboo are tall grasses. Students note these surprising connections beside their list.

The class shares their lists and the teacher records on the board: herbs seen near school or home, and grasses whose seeds we eat. Students observe the range of places where herbs appear — kitchen gardens, roadsides, pots on balconies — and discuss why soft-stemmed plants might grow in these spots rather than in open fields.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and describe the physical features of plants with soft stems and connect familiar food grains to their plant type.
periods.section_context: Mint, tomato, coriander, mustard as herbs; paddy, wheat, bajra, jowar, ragi as seeds of large grasses; sugarcane and bamboo as tall grasses.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Which of these grains does your family eat most — rice, wheat, bajra, jowar, or ragi? Do you know what the plant looks like before it becomes food?' This draws out regional food diversity and links grasses to lived experience.

periods.activity_title: Climbers and Creepers: Plants That Need Support
periods.textbook_anchor: Climbers and Creepers — Students write names of climbers or creepers they have seen and where (p. 54)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations of money plant, jasmine, bottle gourd, watermelon, and pumpkin (p. 53–54)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks students whether they have ever seen a plant growing up a wall, a fence, or another tree. Students share what they noticed — did the plant hold on, or did it lie on the ground? This surface observation sets up the distinction between climbers and creepers before any definition is given.

Students open Textbook p. 53–54 and examine the pictures of climbers and creepers. The teacher explains: climbers grow upward by holding onto something for support; creepers spread along the ground. Students discuss which plants in the pictures they recognise and name them — including any local name they know. The teacher notes that some climbers even draw food from the plant they climb on.

Students write in their notebooks the names of climbers or creepers they have seen and where, noting any local language name, as invited on Textbook p. 54. The teacher prompts: 'Is bottle gourd or pumpkin grown at your home or in a neighbourhood garden — how does it grow?'

Students look at Textbook p. 54 and identify marigold, neem, and jujube — naming each as tree, shrub, climber, or creeper and saying what feature helped them decide. The class discusses their answers, and the teacher draws out that stem type and growth habit are the key clues for classification.

periods.implied_lo: Students can distinguish climbers and creepers from other plant types using observable stem and growth features, and classify familiar plants accordingly.
periods.section_context: Money plant, jasmine, bottle gourd as climbers; watermelon, pumpkin as creepers; marigold, neem, jujube for classification; local language names.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'What does the stem of a money plant or pumpkin plant feel like compared to a tree trunk — and why do you think it cannot stand on its own?' Encourage students to use their own language names for these plants to value regional vocabulary.

periods.activity_title: Plant Spotting Walk: Counting Diversity Near School
periods.textbook_anchor: Climbers and Creepers — Students stand in groups near a tree or shrub and spot as many kinds of plants as they can (p. 54)

time_bands.activity: The teacher gathers the class and explains the outdoor observation task from Textbook p. 54: in small groups of two to four, each group stands near a tree or shrub in or near the school and spots as many plant types as possible — including looking down near their feet.

Groups go outside and observe the plants around their chosen tree or shrub. Students record in their notebooks the plant types they spot — trees, shrubs, herbs, grasses, climbers, creepers — noting the name or a brief description of each. They look in all directions including at the ground level.

The class returns indoors. Each group shares their list: how many different types did they find? The teacher records the collective count on the board, noting which types appeared most often and whether any groups found something unusual.

The teacher asks: 'Was it easy to tell a herb from a grass, or a climber from a creeper, when you were standing outdoors?' Students reflect on which features — stem, growth direction, size — they actually used when classifying a real plant, not a picture.

periods.implied_lo: Students can conduct a structured outdoor observation to identify and count plant diversity in a real environment.
periods.section_context: Trees, shrubs, herbs, grasses, climbers, creepers spotted near school; ground-level plants; group observation and recording.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Before going out, ask: 'What will you look for first — the biggest plants or the smallest?' After the walk, ask: 'Which plant type was hardest to identify and why?' Groups of mixed ability work well here so confident observers can model language for quieter students.

periods.activity_title: Parts of a Plant: Exploring the Tomato Plant
periods.textbook_anchor: Parts of a Plant — Students observe the labelled diagram of a tomato plant and note plant parts (p. 55)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook labelled diagram of a tomato plant showing roots, stem, leaves, flowers, fruits, and seeds (p. 55)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks students to name any part of a plant they can think of — roots, stem, leaf, flower, fruit, seed — and writes each on the board. Students discuss which parts they can see and which are hidden underground, building anticipation for the diagram.

Students open Textbook p. 55 and look at the labelled diagram of a tomato plant. The teacher guides students through each labelled part — roots, stem, leaves, flowers, fruits, seeds — asking students to point to each part and describe what they observe. Students copy the diagram into their notebooks and label the parts.

The teacher draws attention to the leaf diversity shown — peepal, mango, lotus, and khejri leaves on the surrounding pages — and asks students to observe differences in colour, shape, and size. Students note two or three leaf observations beside their diagram: 'Peepal leaves have a long tip; mango leaves are long and narrow.'

The teacher links the plant parts to the tomato plant's role as a herb: its soft stem, its roots in the soil, its fruit we eat. Students name one plant part and say what it does — the stem carries water, the root holds the plant. The unit closes on the idea that every plant part has a job.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify and name the parts of a plant from a diagram and describe observable differences in leaves across plant types.
periods.section_context: Roots, stem, leaves, flowers, fruits, seeds of a tomato plant; peepal, mango, lotus, khejri leaf varieties; colour, shape, size of leaves.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If you pulled a plant gently out of the soil, what do you think you would find at the bottom — and why is that part important?' Let students with kitchen garden experience share observations about roots they may have seen.

periods.activity_title: Making Friends with a Plant: Starting a Plant Observation Record
periods.textbook_anchor: Parts of a Plant — Students choose a plant, name it, and record observations of its leaves, flowers, and fruits in a table (p. 55)
materials: Access to a plant in the school garden or near the school building

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud the invitation from Textbook p. 55: 'Make friends with a plant.' Students discuss what it might mean to befriend a plant — giving it a name, noticing it every day, caring for it. The class talks about why daily observation matters for getting to know any living thing.

Students go out (or move to a window or school garden) and each chooses one plant — preferably a shrub with a thick stem or a small tree — to observe. They name their plant, then look closely at its leaves, flowers, and fruits, noting: are there many, a few, or none? Students record their first observations in the table format shown on Textbook p. 55.

Back in the classroom, the teacher reads aloud the follow-up questions from Textbook p. 56: Are new leaves growing? Do old leaves fall? Are there flowers or fruit? Students add any further observations they noticed during their time with the plant to their notebook record.

Pairs share what they noticed about their chosen plant and compare: did both plants have flowers? Were the leaves the same colour? The teacher asks: 'What is one thing you noticed about your plant that surprised you?' Students note this in their record as a personal observation.

periods.implied_lo: Students can carry out a structured observation of a living plant and record findings in an organised table.
periods.section_context: Chosen plant (shrub or tree near school); leaves, flowers, fruits counted and described; plant named by student; first observation record.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'What is the most interesting thing about the plant you chose — why did you pick that one?' Encourage students who chose the same plant to compare their notes and see whether they noticed different things, introducing the idea that careful observation is a skill that improves with practice.

periods.activity_title: Leaf Observation: Draw, Describe, and Discover
periods.textbook_anchor: Parts of a Plant — Students observe leaves in their surroundings, draw, colour, and label them, then describe them to a classmate (p. 57)
materials: A few collected leaves of different shapes if available in the school environment
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations of varied leaf types (p. 57)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks students to look at Textbook p. 57 and name as many different leaf shapes as they can see. Students then step outside briefly or look through a window to pick two or three leaves (fallen or from a plant they can access). They bring the leaves back to their desk for the drawing activity.

Students open their notebooks and draw, colour, and label each leaf they have collected or observed, as invited on Textbook p. 57. Beside each drawing they write brief notes on colour, shape, size, texture, and smell. The teacher circulates, prompting: 'What does the edge of the leaf look like — smooth or jagged? Does it have a smell when you hold it?'

Students pair up and describe their drawn leaves to their partner without showing the drawing — the partner tries to picture the leaf from the description alone. Then they switch. The class shares a few examples: what did they include in their description that really helped their partner?

The teacher invites the class to make a collective statement: 'What can we say about leaves after doing this activity?' Students suggest observations — leaves vary in shape, size, colour, and texture — and the teacher records them on the board. This consolidates the generalisation that leaf diversity is one of the most visible signs of plant diversity.

periods.implied_lo: Students can present detailed observations of natural objects through drawing, labelling, and oral description.
periods.section_context: Leaves from school surroundings; colour, shape, size, texture, and smell of leaves; drawing, labelling, and oral description to a classmate.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Can you describe your leaf so clearly that I could draw it without seeing it?' Pair students of different drawing confidence so that oral description becomes an equally valued way of sharing — not just those who draw well.

periods.activity_title: Blindfold Fruit Smell Game and Bark Rubbing
periods.textbook_anchor: Parts of a Plant — Students blindfold themselves and identify fruit by smell from a distance, then repeat with cut fruit (p. 57)
materials: Two or three whole fruits (e.g. lemon, orange, guava)
Cut pieces of the same fruits on a plate
A soft cloth for a blindfold

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the experiment from Textbook p. 57: one student is blindfolded while a partner slowly brings a whole fruit close. The blindfolded student says when they first detect the smell. The teacher asks the class to predict: will whole or cut fruit be easier to detect by smell, and from further away?

In pairs, students take turns as the blindfolded student and the one holding the fruit, working with both whole and cut versions of each fruit available. Students note in their notebooks: which fruit they detected first, from roughly how close, and whether the cut version was easier or harder to recognise. The teacher asks: 'Was the smell stronger when the fruit was cut? What do you think changed?'

The class gathers to share results. The teacher records on the board which fruit most pairs detected earliest and at the greatest distance. Students discuss why cut fruit might smell more strongly — connecting to the idea that the inside of a fruit carries more scent than the skin. Students also name the fruits in their home language.

The teacher links the fruit smell experiment back to plant parts: fruits carry seeds, and strong smells attract animals to eat the fruit and spread seeds. Students note this in their notebooks as a one-sentence observation connecting smell to the fruit's job in the plant's life.

periods.implied_lo: Students can design and carry out a simple comparative investigation using the sense of smell and record what changes between conditions.
periods.section_context: Whole fruits and cut fruit pieces; blindfold smell-identification at varying distances; comparison of whole versus cut fruit scent intensity; fruit smell and seed dispersal connection.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Which fruit was hardest to identify and which was easiest — and does that match what you expected before the experiment?' Ensure the blindfold activity is done gently and that students feel comfortable; offer an option to keep eyes closed without a cloth if preferred.

periods.activity_title: Bark Rubbing: Reading a Tree Through Touch and Pattern
periods.textbook_anchor: Parts of a Plant — Students make bark rubbings, label them, and try to identify the tree from its bark pattern (p. 59)
materials: Access to one or two trees near the school building

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks students to close their eyes and imagine touching the outside of a tree trunk — is it smooth or rough, flat or ridged? Students share their sensory memories. The teacher introduces the bark rubbing activity from Textbook p. 59: pressing paper against bark and rubbing a crayon over it to capture the surface pattern.

Students go outside with a sheet of paper and a crayon. Each student chooses a tree, presses the paper against the bark, and makes a rubbing. They also look closely at the bark surface — noting any animals, insects, mosses, or markings. On the reverse of the paper they write the name or description of the tree. Students return to the classroom with their rubbings.

All bark-rubbing sheets are collected and spread out. Students look at the rubbings from the front — without seeing the name on the reverse — and try to guess which tree each rubbing came from, as described on Textbook p. 59. The class discusses which patterns were easy to match and which were hard, and what features of bark they now notice that they had not paid attention to before.

The teacher draws out that bark is the hard outer covering that protects the trunk, and that it varies between trees just as leaves do. Students note one observation about bark texture in their notebooks, reinforcing that trees can be identified through multiple sensory clues — not just leaves or fruits.

periods.implied_lo: Students can collect physical evidence through a hands-on technique and use it to identify and compare natural objects.
periods.section_context: Bark of trees near school; bark rubbing with paper and crayon; bark texture observation; animals or insects found on bark; identification of tree from bark pattern.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If you could only use your bark rubbing to identify a tree — no leaves, no fruit — what clues would you look for?' Encourage students who find rubbings of the same tree to compare their sheets and notice how even the same tree shows variation.

periods.activity_title: Leaf Rangoli and Plant Reflection: Celebrating What We Know
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students collect fallen leaves and flowers, arrange them as rangoli patterns, and create animal shapes from leaves (p. 61)
materials: Fallen leaves and flowers collected from the school ground
periods.visual_aids: Textbook reflection prompts and leaf rangoli example (p. 60–61)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 60 and leads a whole-class discussion on the three questions: What would happen if there were no plants? How does the root help a plant grow? What is the role of the stem? Students share their ideas freely, with the teacher drawing out the connection between plant parts and survival.

Students write in their notebooks the list of plants they have seen in school, a park, or near home — naming the type (tree, shrub, herb, grass, climber, or creeper) — and note which part of the plant helped them identify its type, as invited on Textbook p. 60. They also write two or three sentences describing their favourite plant and why it is their favourite.

Students go outside briefly to collect fallen leaves and flowers from the school ground (no plant is damaged). Back at their desks, students arrange the collected leaves and flowers into a rangoli pattern or create an animal shape from leaves, as invited on Textbook p. 61. The activity connects plant observation to a living Indian artistic tradition that uses natural materials.

Students display their leaf rangoli on their desks or on the floor. The class does a quick gallery walk — looking at each other's arrangements. The teacher closes by asking: 'Which plant or part of a plant did you find most surprising or beautiful in this chapter?' Students share one word or phrase each.

periods.implied_lo: Students can express their understanding of plant diversity through a creative arrangement and support a discussion about the importance of plants with specific examples.
periods.section_context: Fallen leaves and flowers from school ground; rangoli and animal shapes from leaves; importance of plants discussion; root and stem roles; favourite plant description; plant-type classification list.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Rangoli is often made during festivals using flowers and colours — what other natural materials do people in your family or community use for decoration?' This draws out regional craft traditions connected to plants without labelling the tradition explicitly.

assessment_items.question_text: Riya walks to school and sees a very tall plant. It has one big, hard trunk and many branches with leaves. She can feel that the bark is rough. What type of plant is this?

options.label: A
options.text: A climber, because it grows tall

options.label: B
options.text: A herb, because it grows in the ground

options.label: C
options.text: A shrub, because it has many branches

options.label: D
options.text: A tree, because it has one big woody trunk and deep roots

assessment_items.annotation: Award the mark for option B. The question tests whether students use the single woody trunk as the defining feature of a tree, not height or the presence of branches or leaves.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can recall and describe familiar plants in their surroundings using sensory details and location.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student is using 'many branches' as the criterion for a shrub, overlooking that a tree also has branches — the key difference is the single large woody trunk.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student associates height with climbing, confusing the growth habit of a climber (needing support to grow upward) with simply being tall.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student is using 'grows in the ground' as a criterion for a herb, not recognising that all plants grow in the ground and that herbs are defined by their soft stems.

assessment_items.question_text: Mohan's mother uses tulsi leaves to make tea and adds curry leaves to cooking. His family also eats moong dal almost every day. Write two ways in which shrubs are useful to Mohan's family.
expected_elements: Names or references tulsi or curry leaf as a shrub used for food or medicine (e.g. tulsi tea, curry leaf in cooking).
States that moong dal (or another dal such as toor, masoor, or urad) comes from a shrub, showing the connection between pulses and shrub plants.
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark for each expected element; two marks total. Accept any correct dal (toor, masoor, moong, urad) as evidence of the shrub-pulse connection. Regionally varied examples of shrubs used in cooking are acceptable and correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can distinguish shrubs from trees using observable physical features and connect plant types to everyday uses.

assessment_items.question_text: Paddy, wheat, and bajra are all important foods eaten across India. Which statement about these plants is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Paddy, wheat, and bajra are all trees with hard woody trunks.

options.label: B
options.text: Paddy, wheat, and bajra are climbers that grow on fences.

options.label: C
options.text: Paddy, wheat, and bajra are seeds of large grasses.

options.label: D
options.text: Paddy, wheat, and bajra are seeds of shrubs, like dal.

assessment_items.annotation: Award the mark for option B. The item tests whether students retain the surprising link between staple food grains and the grass plant type.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and describe the physical features of plants with soft stems and connect familiar food grains to their plant type.

competency.competency_text: Describes usage of natural resources in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student is applying the tree category to large or important food plants, not recognising that trees are defined by a single woody trunk and that grasses can be tall without being trees.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student confuses height or dependency (climbing) with the grass category — possibly because grasses grow in fields rather than pots, but climbing is an unrelated growth habit.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student correctly recalls the shrub-dal connection from the Shrubs section but incorrectly extends it to grains, conflating two different plant types and their food products.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at these two plants: Plant X has a thin, flexible stem and grows upward by holding on to a fence. Plant Y has a thin, flexible stem and spreads along the ground. Write the correct type for each plant and name one example of each type.
expected_elements: Identifies Plant X as a climber and gives a correct example (e.g. money plant, jasmine, bottle gourd).
Identifies Plant Y as a creeper and gives a correct example (e.g. watermelon, pumpkin).
States or implies that the key difference is the direction of growth — upward with support versus along the ground.
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark per expected element; three marks total. Accept any locally known climber or creeper as a valid example — regional variation is expected and correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can distinguish climbers and creepers from other plant types using observable stem and growth features, and classify familiar plants accordingly.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes diversity among plants, and birds and animals in their immediate environment (shape, sounds, food habits, growth, habitat)

assessment_items.question_text: During the outdoor plant-spotting activity, Priya's group stood near a neem tree and found six different types of plants around them. They saw grasses near their feet, a creeper on the wall, and herbs in a crack in the ground. Write two things a student should look for to tell a herb apart from a grass when observing plants outdoors.
expected_elements: Notes that a herb has a soft stem that does not become woody, while a grass has a thin, often flat or hollow-stemmed leaf structure.

Mentions a visible feature that helps distinguish them outdoors, such as the shape or texture of the stem, or the appearance of the leaves (thin flat blades for grasses versus broader softer leaves for many herbs).
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark per expected element; two marks total. Students do not need to use scientific vocabulary precisely — what matters is that the observable features they name are accurate and actionable for outdoor identification.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can conduct a structured outdoor observation to identify and count plant diversity in a real environment.

assessment_items.question_text: A tomato plant has roots, a stem, leaves, flowers, fruits, and seeds. What is the main job of the roots?

options.label: A
options.text: To carry water and food from the soil to the rest of the plant, and to hold the plant firmly in the ground

options.label: B
options.text: To hold the flowers so that fruits can form

options.label: C
options.text: To make food for the plant using sunlight

options.label: D
options.text: To protect the plant from animals by going deep into the ground

assessment_items.annotation: Award the mark for option A. The question anchors to the tomato plant diagram and the root-and-stem discussion in the Parts of a Plant section.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify and name the parts of a plant from a diagram and describe observable differences in leaves across plant types.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student is attributing photosynthesis (making food from sunlight) to the root rather than the leaf — a common confusion between the functions of different plant parts.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student is merging the function of the stem (which supports flowers and fruits) with that of the root, not distinguishing the roles of these two parts.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student recognises that roots go deep but assigns them a protective function against animals rather than the anchoring and water-absorption function.

assessment_items.question_text: Ananya chose a hibiscus shrub in the school garden to observe closely. She named it 'Pinky.' She looked at its leaves, flowers, and fruits and recorded her observations in a table. Write two things Ananya should include in her observation table to make her record useful.
expected_elements: Notes whether there are many, a few, or no leaves on the plant at the time of observation.
Notes whether flowers or fruits are present or absent, with any observable detail such as colour or number.
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark per expected element; two marks total. Accept equivalent phrasing — the key is that the student names specific observable data points (presence/absence and quantity or description of leaves, flowers, or fruits) rather than vague statements.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can carry out a structured observation of a living plant and record findings in an organised table.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

Notes whether flowers or fruits are present or absent, with any observable detail such as colour or number.

assessment_items.task: Choose two leaves from your surroundings — they can be different shapes or sizes. Draw each leaf in your notebook and label it with the name of the plant if you know it. Write two sentences describing what you notice about each leaf — include at least one detail about its colour, shape, texture, or smell.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Leaf 1: Draw here. Name of plant (if known): ___. What I notice: (1) ___ (2) ___.
Leaf 2: Draw here. Name of plant (if known): ___. What I notice: (1) ___ (2) ___.
format_of_output: Two leaf drawings with labels in the student's notebook
Two sentences of observation per leaf
assessment_items.annotation: Assess the drawing for observable accuracy (not artistic quality) and the written observations for specificity — a strong response names a concrete sensory detail (e.g. 'the edge is jagged', 'it has a strong smell when I crush it') rather than a generic statement ('it is green and has leaves'). Students may name leaves in any language.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can present detailed observations of natural objects through drawing, labelling, and oral description.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can transfer leaf-observation skills to real leaves in their immediate environment, capturing meaningful sensory details through both drawing and written description.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold separates the two leaves clearly and prompts both visual (drawing) and written (observations) output — look for whether the student has used both modes and whether the written detail goes beyond colour alone.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: Drawing shows leaf outline with visible features (veins, edge shape); written observations name at least one specific sensory detail beyond colour. Weak: Drawing is approximate and observations are generic ('it is a leaf, it is green').
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who cannot yet write in full sentences may draw arrows pointing to features and label them with single words. Students with limited access to outdoor leaves may use leaves illustrated in the textbook as the basis for their drawing.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: This format directly mirrors the textbook activity and allows students to demonstrate both observational accuracy and descriptive language simultaneously.

assessment_items.question_text: During the blindfold fruit-smell experiment, most students found that cut fruit was easier to identify by smell than whole fruit. Give one reason why cut fruit might have a stronger smell, and write one question you would want to investigate next based on this experiment.
expected_elements: Gives a plausible reason why cut fruit smells more strongly — for example, that cutting opens up the inside of the fruit where the smell is stronger, or that more of the fruit's surface is exposed to the air.

States a new investigation question related to smell or fruit — for example, 'Does a larger piece of cut fruit smell stronger than a smaller piece?' or 'Which fruit can be smelled from the furthest distance?'
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark per expected element; two marks total. Accept any scientifically reasonable explanation for stronger smell in cut fruit. Accept any genuine new inquiry question related to the experiment — precision of scientific vocabulary is not required at this level.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can design and carry out a simple comparative investigation using the sense of smell and record what changes between conditions.

assessment_items.question_text: Kiran made bark rubbings of three different trees in the school garden. After looking only at the rubbings (not the trees), she and her classmates tried to match each rubbing to the correct tree. Write two things about bark that a student could look for in the rubbing to help identify the tree.
expected_elements: Names an observable pattern or texture feature visible in a bark rubbing — for example, the depth of ridges (deep or shallow), the direction of lines (vertical, criss-cross, circular), or the roughness of the surface.
Notes that different trees have different bark patterns, so comparing rubbings can help tell them apart — showing understanding that bark is a distinguishing feature.
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark per expected element; two marks total. Accept any accurate observable bark feature. The response does not need to name specific trees — the focus is on using bark patterns as an identification tool.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can collect physical evidence through a hands-on technique and use it to identify and compare natural objects.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: Names an observable pattern or texture feature visible in a bark rubbing — for example, the depth of ridges (deep or shallow), the direction of lines (vertical, criss-cross, circular), or the roughness of the surface.
Notes that different trees have different bark patterns, so comparing rubbings can help tell them apart — showing understanding that bark is a distinguishing feature.

assessment_items.task: Collect five to eight fallen leaves or flower petals from the school ground. Arrange them on your desk to make a rangoli pattern or the shape of an animal. In your notebook, write the names of the plants the leaves or flowers came from (use your local language name if you do not know the English name). Below the names, write two sentences about why plants matter to us.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My rangoli / animal shape uses leaves or flowers from: ___.
Plants matter to us because: (1) ___ (2) ___.
format_of_output: A leaf-and-flower rangoli or animal arrangement on the desk
A written list of plant names in the notebook
Two sentences about the importance of plants
assessment_items.annotation: Assess the creative arrangement for intentional placement (not randomness) and the written responses for specificity — a strong response names concrete reasons (food, shade, air, beauty, medicine) rather than 'plants are good'. Plant names in any language are accepted and valued. Regional and locally known plants are expected and correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can express their understanding of plant diversity through a creative arrangement and support a discussion about the importance of plants with specific examples.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can combine creative expression using natural materials with reflective writing about why plants matter, drawing on everything encountered across the chapter.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Look for whether the arrangement is intentional and whether the written reasons move beyond a single idea — students who write both a food reason and a shelter or environmental reason show richer understanding.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: Arrangement shows a recognisable pattern or shape; at least two distinct reasons for plant importance are given with specific detail (e.g. 'we eat wheat which is a grass' or 'trees give shade when we walk to school'). Weak: Leaves are placed randomly; reasons are vague ('plants give us life').
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who cannot yet write full sentences may draw a simple image alongside each reason. Students who struggle with fine motor arrangement may describe their intended pattern in words. Any language is accepted for plant names.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Creative physical arrangement and written reflection
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The rangoli activity mirrors a living Indian art tradition using natural materials, and the written reflection ensures the creative act is paired with explicit articulation of plant importance.
